Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Stratosphere Industries Q3 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, ladies and gentlemen, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Stratosphere Industries' Q3 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Elena Vasquez, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Thornton, Chief Financial Officer; and Sarah Kline, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning. Stratosphere Industries delivered a solid performance in Q3, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering value to our shareholders. I will cover the following areas: robust revenue growth across our commercial aerospace, defense, and services segments; accelerating commercial aircraft delivery rates amid a strong recovery trajectory; sustained R&D investments in next-generation platforms and technologies; and our disciplined capital deployment strategy.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our NGAD program and its potential to secure air dominance for decades to come. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily. With that, I'll turn it over to Michael for a deeper dive into our financial results.

Michael Thornton:
Thank you, Elena, and good morning, everyone. As we discussed in our prepared remarks, we delivered another quarter of strong top-line growth, with consolidated revenues reaching $26.4 billion, up 14% year-over-year. This performance was driven by robust demand across all three of our core segments: Commercial Aerospace, Defense, and Services. I'll now walk you through the segment details, including year-over-year percentage changes, key drivers, and forward-looking insights.

Starting with Commercial Aerospace, which accounted for 42% of total revenues at $11.1 billion, up a robust 28% year-over-year. This segment continues to benefit from the sustained global recovery in air travel, with revenue passenger kilometers now exceeding pre-pandemic levels by 5% according to IATA data. Our OEM deliveries were a highlight, with widebody aircraft shipments including strong volumes of A350s and 787 Dreamliners under multiyear agreements with key customers like Emirates, Qatar Airways, and Delta. Narrowbody production also ramped efficiently, led by our 737 MAX family, which saw a significant delivery increase amid industry-wide supply chain stabilization.

Regionally, North America contributed 45% of segment growth, fueled by U.S. low-cost carriers like Southwest and United expanding fleets to meet domestic leisure demand. Europe was up 35% YoY, supported by Lufthansa Group's orders and Ryanair's aggressive narrowbody expansion, while Asia-Pacific—our highest-growth region at 42% YoY—benefited from China's reopening and IndiGo's massive A320neo order book. Middle East carriers added another 25% uplift via 777X certification milestones.

On the technical front, our investments in sustainable aviation technologies are paying dividends. We've integrated 15% more sustainable aviation fuel-compatible engines across our CFM56 and LEAP portfolios, aligning with ICAO's CORSIA offset requirements and positioning us ahead of the EU's ReFuelEU mandate. Supply chain headwinds persist—titanium pricing up 20% due to geopolitical sourcing shifts from Russia—but our dual-sourcing strategy with U.S. and Japanese suppliers has mitigated delays, keeping our 12-month delivery backlog at a record $185 billion, up 22% YoY. Margins expanded 220 basis points to 12.8%, driven by favorable mix and pricing discipline on aftermarket parts. Looking ahead, we expect continued 20-25% growth in 2025 as widebody production scales.

Moving to Defense, which represented 48% of revenues at $12.7 billion, up a steady 7% year-over-year. This segment remains our bedrock, underpinned by a $142 billion funded backlog—up 9% YoY—and multi-year U.S. DoD contracts insulated from commercial cyclicality. Fixed-wing platforms drove 40% of growth, with F-35 Lot 16/17 low-rate initial production deliveries generating significant revenue, including sensor fusion upgrades for Block 4 capabilities. Our sustainment revenue from the F-35 fleet benefited from the ALIS-to-ODIN transition and a 95% mission-capable rate target.

Missiles and hypersonics were standout performers, up 18% to $3.1 billion, led by JASSM-ER and LRASM ramps for the U.S. Navy's Distributed Maritime Operations concept. The Ground Based Strategic Deterrent program—our next-gen ICBM replacement for Minuteman III—secured additional funding, with first flight tests on track for 2026. Unmanned systems grew 12%, highlighted by MQ-9 Reaper exports to NATO allies amid Ukraine-related demand surges.

Regionally, U.S. revenues rose 6%, anchored by the FY24 NDAA's $886 billion topline. International sales jumped 12%, with FMS deals to Poland for F-16 upgrades and Saudi Arabia for THAAD batteries offsetting slower European volumes due to AUKUS delays. APAC was up 15%, driven by Japan's GCAP collaboration on next-gen fighters. Technically, we're advancing digital engineering via Model-Based Systems Engineering, reducing design cycles by 30% on our NGAD demonstrator. Margins held at 11.5%, with 80 basis points of expansion from performance fees on legacy programs like the B-21 Raider. Strategically, geopolitical tensions—U.S.-China straits risks and Middle East escalations—are extending program lives and boosting unexercised international remaining performance obligations by 14%. We guide to low-double-digit growth through 2026, with backlog conversion at 25% annually.

Finally, Services, our highest-margin segment at 10% of revenues with $2.6 billion, up 11% year-over-year. This reflects strength in MRO, upgrades, and digital services across both commercial and defense fleets. Commercial aftermarket was up 16%, driven by a 20% increase in shop visits for aging A320ceo and 737NG fleets, with our Mobile Fleet Services division logging 1.2 million flight hours supported. Defense sustainment grew 9%, including performance-based logistics contracts for C-130J Hercules and F-22 depot overhauls.

Regionally, EMEA led with 14% growth via Lufthansa Technik partnerships and Etihad's A380 heavy checks, while North America benefited from USAF's Contractor Logistics Support Services awards. APAC MRO demand surged 18% from high-utilization fleets at AirAsia and ANA. Key initiatives include our TrueChoice Overhaul+ program, which leverages predictive analytics and AI-driven digital twins to cut turnaround times by 25% and boost availability to 99%. We've also rolled out AR-enhanced technician workflows, reducing error rates by 15% per FAA audits.

Margins expanded 150 basis points to 18.2%, reflecting scale in our global network of 28 MRO facilities and a shift to higher-value digital services, now 22% of segment mix. Our services backlog stands at $28 billion, up 13% YoY, providing visibility amid OEM production ramps. We see mid-teens growth persisting, as fleets age—global average aircraft age now 13.5 years—and regulatory pushes like EASA's enhanced airworthiness directives drive upgrades.

In summary, our segment performance underscores the resilience of our diversified portfolio: Commercial's post-pandemic rebound, Defense's geopolitical tailwinds, and Services' annuity-like stability. Total backlog now exceeds $355 billion, with book-to-bill at 1.3x. Earnings per share were $3.25, and we continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $6.8 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year remains unchanged at 13-15% revenue growth and 18% EPS expansion. We're on track to outperform peers amid industry-wide challenges like labor shortages and inflation.

Building on this strong foundation, let me provide more detail on our commercial aircraft delivery rates and recovery trajectory. In Q3, we achieved 48 commercial aircraft deliveries, a 30% increase from the 37 units in Q3 2023 and marking our strongest quarterly performance in recent years. This included 36 single-aisle 737 MAX variants—our workhorse, accounting for 75% of deliveries—and 12 widebodies, split between 787 Dreamliners and 777X freighters. Year-to-date, we're at 126 deliveries, putting us on track for our full-year guidance of 160 to 180 units, which implies an average monthly rate of 14 to 15 aircraft in the back half. For context, pre-pandemic peaks saw us averaging 45 to 52 deliveries per month; we're now at about 75% of that level, with clear momentum.

This progress reflects a deliberate ramp-up strategy we've been executing. Our final assembly lines are now operating at 85% capacity utilization, up significantly, thanks to investments in automation and workforce expansion. We've added thousands of direct production hires year-to-date, and implemented digital thread technologies to reduce assembly touch labor by 22% on the 737 line. These initiatives have shaved cycle times per aircraft, positioning us to hit higher monthly deliveries by next year.

Industry-wide, we're seeing a robust rebound, with global OEM deliveries strong. Narrowbody demand remains insatiable, fueled by low-cost carrier expansion and replacement cycles. Widebody recovery is progressing steadily, supported by long-haul premium travel resurgence, though constrained by supply disruptions like titanium shortages and engine issues. Regionally, Asia-Pacific is the growth engine at 45% of deliveries, with major orders from Chinese and Indian carriers. Middle East carriers took a solid share of widebodies, while North America and Europe face some constraints from pilot shortages and economic pressures. Our visibility remains strong with thousands of unfilled slots through 2030.

Challenges like supply chain bottlenecks persist, capping output below plan, but our defense heritage ensures high on-time parts delivery. Strategically, we're leveraging synergies, with capex supporting expansions and advanced materials from defense programs. Looking ahead, we see delivery rates accelerating, with backlog conversion providing revenue visibility. EPS accretion from commercial remains a key driver.

Next, I'd like to dive into our R&D investments, which remain a cornerstone of our long-term growth strategy in the Aerospace & Defense sector. In Q3, we deployed $2.4 billion in R&D expenses, representing 9.2% of our total revenue—up 12% year-over-year. For the full year, we continue to guide toward roughly 8.5% to 9% of projected revenues, outpacing the industry average.

This investment split is approximately 55% independent research and development, funded internally to maintain leadership, and 45% customer-funded, tied to major primes like the DoD, NASA, and international partners. We're prioritizing next-generation platforms and disruptive technologies to address great power competition, supply chain resilience, and digital engineering.

Our largest allocation targets sixth-generation fighter ecosystems, including NGAD. We've advanced digital twin simulations for the NGAD demonstrator to high TRL, achieving strong fidelity in hypersonic flow modeling using proprietary tools integrated with leading software. This positions us for upcoming DoD contracts. We're also investing in Collaborative Combat Aircraft, with our prototype completing autonomous swarm flight tests demonstrating reduced pilot workload.

Hypersonics captured a significant share, with solid-fuel scramjet achievements in ground tests supporting key Air Force pipelines. On directed energy, we're advancing high-power lasers for air defense, with strong test results. Space R&D focuses on proliferated LEO constellations and reusable launch tech, supporting SDA awards and NASA missions. Autonomy and AI efforts include sensor fusion and MBSE migrations, slashing design iterations, plus quantum-resistant cybersecurity.

Geographically, it's U.S.-centric with growth in Indo-Pacific via AUKUS and FMS, and Europe through GCAP. These investments de-risk our backlog, with margins improving on new awards. Tailwinds from budget growth outweigh risks like sequestration. In summary, our R&D ensures we lead the pivot to attritable, autonomous capabilities, positioning for strong organic growth.

As we wrap up our Q3 results, I want to spend some time on our capital deployment strategy, which remains a cornerstone of delivering superior shareholder returns in this dynamic Aerospace & Defense landscape. We're guided by a disciplined framework: first, invest in high-return organic growth opportunities like our classified programs and next-gen tech; second, maintain a rock-solid balance sheet with investment-grade ratings—currently A- from S&P and A3 from Moody's; and third, return excess capital to shareholders via dividends, share repurchases, and bolt-on acquisitions that enhance our technological edge and market position.

On dividends, it's a top priority, reflecting the predictability of our defense backlog—now at a record $145 billion, up 12% year-over-year, with 45% funded and visibility extending to 2030 on programs like F-35 sustainment and LRASM production. We've increased our quarterly dividend by 10% this year to $0.75 per share, or $3.00 annualized, marking our 22nd consecutive annual hike. This delivers a forward yield of 1.8%, with a conservative payout ratio of 28% on adjusted EPS—well below our 40-50% target, giving flexibility amid inflation.

Looking ahead, we expect 8-10% annual growth over the next three years, supported by free cash flow conversion north of 95% this year—$4.2 billion generated in the first nine months, despite supply chain disruptions in titanium forgings. This positions us competitively, preserving firepower for growth.

On share repurchases, we're executing opportunistically within our $5 billion authorization. Year-to-date, we've repurchased 18 million shares for $1.8 billion at an average price of $248—about 5% below current levels—driving 120 basis points of EPS accretion in Q3. We've retired 4% of our float over 12 months, enhancing ROIC from 14.2% to 15.1%.

We have $3.2 billion remaining and expect to deploy $2-2.5 billion in 2024, pausing above 18x forward EV/EBITDA to prioritize M&A. This has outperformed in volatile markets.

M&A leans into tailwinds like hypersonics and autonomy. Our $10 billion war chest—$6.8 billion cash plus undrawn revolver—funds this at 1.2x net debt to EBITDA. This quarter, we closed the $1.9 billion acquisition of SkyForge Dynamics, adding $450 million backlog including Space Force contracts, accreting to EPS post-synergies. We've captured 70% of run-rate savings.

Pipeline is robust: term sheets on $800 million tuck-ins in UAS autonomy and directed energy, aligning with DoD's Replicator and Indo-Pacific commitments. U.S. DoD is 85% of revenues, but EMEA up 18% on F-35 production, Asia-Pacific 22% CAGR.

In summary, we prioritize ROIC above 15%, top-quartile TSR, and positioning for a $1 trillion market. Inflation pressures are mitigated by pricing clauses, with geopolitics driving 7-9% organic growth. Our 92% defense mix insulates us.

Our specific financial highlights include gross margin of 13.2%, operating income of $3.8 billion, and Q3 free cash flow of $1.5 billion. We're actively managing costs, investing in growth, and returning capital through dividends and repurchases.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Josh Friedman with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Josh Friedman:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the R&D investments in hypersonics and NGAD programs?

Elena Vasquez:
Certainly, Josh. As Michael outlined, we've made substantial progress on hypersonics with Mach 5+ scramjet tests and high-power lasers showing excellent lethality. For NGAD, our digital twins and CCA prototypes like Specter are advancing rapidly, de-risking future contracts and reducing pilot workload significantly. These align with DoD priorities and our funded backlog.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Carter with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about updates on the capital deployment plans, particularly the M&A pipeline?

Michael Thornton:
Emily, great question. Our pipeline remains strong with those two tuck-ins totaling $800 million in UAS and directed energy, perfectly timed for Replicator and AUKUS. The SkyForge deal is already delivering synergies, and we'll continue opportunistic buybacks while growing the dividend at 8-10%. Discipline is key—we stay below our valuation benchmarks.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

David Lee:
Thanks. Regarding the commercial aerospace recovery and delivery rates outlook?

Elena Vasquez:
David, we're accelerating with 48 deliveries in Q3 and on pace for the high end of guidance. Supply chain improvements and workforce ramps have us nearing pre-pandemic rates, with Asia-Pacific leading demand. Backlog visibility through 2030 and synergies from defense keep us confident in 20-25% segment growth next year.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
